title: From Crystallization to the Ontology Boundary
subtitle: When can a machine turn experience into a small, exact theory of its world?
excerpt: Thirty-eight experiments on automata learning, symbolic planning, abstraction, ontology discovery, and exact checking.
lede: The idea was this: ask a world questions, turn its answers into a small theory that can run as code, and repair the theory whenever reality contradicts it. This worked surprisingly well when I gave the learner a clear set of states, a rule language, a reset button, or a precise way to check its answer. Then I removed those supports. The learner could no longer reliably discover the states, recover the transition graph, transfer old rules, or recognize something new. That failure does not erase the earlier results. It tells us exactly what those results depend on.

entries.label: Entry 01
entries.title: Small exact theories could be recovered, but abstraction helped only under the right conditions.
entries.dek: The first set asks whether contradictions can repair an automaton, whether several worlds can share one description, and whether a neural model's behavior can be turned into symbols.

blocks.markdown:
**Can contradictions repair a bad automaton?** The starting NFA had 22 states, 64 arcs, and bounded accuracy 0.9663. After 299 membership questions and two repair rounds, the learner found an exact 9-state theory. A capacity-limited version also worked. It differed by one arc, and I leave that difference visible because I cannot explain it.

**Did the capacity limit cause the repair?** A second test began with a Mealy machine of complexity 24. Two rounds reduced it to the exact world: six states and twelve arcs. But the version without a capacity limit followed exactly the same path. In this run, the limit had **no measurable causal effect**.

**Can several renamed worlds share one theory?** Yes, when they really are the same underneath. The W-method tests found one hidden six-state machine behind four renamed views. The description shrank from 392 bits for separate models to 215 bits, and every hidden action translation was recovered. Unrelated worlds stayed separate. With a supplied register-program language, four related 436-bit tables became one 138-bit `(2,3)` coordinate program; unrelated tables were again rejected.

**Can a useful Boolean vocabulary be learned?** Sometimes. Paid NAND-based macros recovered the planted mechanism in 8 of 9 families. For related tasks, code cost fell to 0.521 of baseline. But the confidence interval for evaluation count still included no improvement, and unrelated tasks became worse at 1.792 times the baseline evaluation cost. In sequential worlds, two correct reusable gates cut transfer cost from 21 to 6, evaluations from 73,876 to 3,480, and queries from 12 to 8.33. A larger study found that meaning and price strongly interacted. It also disproved two predictions: a disjoint vocabulary helped a little instead of hurting, and an expensive correct vocabulary did not come close enough to baseline.

**When should a learned library be trusted?** An early endpoint said the library was MDL-positive everywhere. That was misleading. In the corrected XOR/XNOR experiment, support for the true library collapsed as unrelated data and noise increased. With fully related data, target optimality fell from 1.00 at zero noise to 0.03 at 20% noise. Whenever the target library truly was the global optimum, the greedy search found it. The problem was lack of evidence, not failure of local search.

**Can symbols be extracted from a neural model?** Symbolic regression recovered `force/mass` from the analytic system and from three trained black boxes, while rejecting a random-network control. The macros did not reduce the stable number of queries. In another test, a five-state DFA extracted from each of three imperfect transformers was perfect on the sampled hidden-language test while still matching each transformer's mistakes on long sequences. That is useful denoising on a bounded test. It is not a proof for every possible sequence length.

blocks.alt: Bar chart comparing three transformers and their extracted symbolic DFAs on bounded and long hidden-language accuracy, beside the five-state extracted DFA graph.
blocks.caption: On the sampled long test, the extracted five-state DFAs matched the hidden language perfectly while the neural models still made mistakes. This shows symbolic denoising on this test, not equivalence at every possible length.
blocks.provenance: Original embedded PNG from NFAWorldModel.ipynb, source cell 14 (tiny transformer to symbolic DFA).

blocks.markdown:
**Does a neural arithmetic learner pass through a simple intermediate theory?** In one seed, I extracted the exact five-state ADD/SUB machine from a recurrent neural model. Across ten seeds, the first exact machines appeared at epochs 10–19, often before the neural model stayed above .99 accuracy. But the preregistered four-state carry/borrow waypoint appeared in **0 of 10 seeds**.

A paired learning-rate test gave the same answer: zero canonical waypoints in 20 arms. Slow learning often produced too few states. Fast learning more often went directly to an exact machine or split into too many states. In 6 of 9 eligible fast arms, a faithful exact machine appeared before neural mastery. Many intermediate machines hit the state limit or were exactly wrong even when sampled neural accuracy was high. A planned deterministic FP32 rerun never started because the archived source had a syntax error.

blocks.alt: Three-panel paired learning-rate result showing extracted state complexity, predeclared outcome fractions for slow and fast arms, and faithful exact recovery step versus neural mastery step.
blocks.caption: The proposed four-state waypoint did not appear. Slow runs more often used too few states; fast runs more often went straight to an exact machine or used too many. In the right panel, points below the diagonal are cases where neural mastery came first.
blocks.provenance: Original embedded PNG from NFAWorldModel.ipynb, source cell 17 (paired learning-rate claim-closing experiment).

groups.title: Supported in these controlled worlds
items: Contradiction-driven finite-state learners can replace larger inherited theories with compact exact observable models.
MDL can recognize shared structure across renamed interfaces and pay for abstractions that transfer to related synthetic tasks.
Symbolic extraction can denoise a neural endpoint when the behavioral class and verification interface are controlled.

groups.title: Not supported
items: The model-capacity intervention caused the observed Mealy recovery.
Learned vocabularies universally reduce search cost or help unrelated tasks.
Neural arithmetic learning passes through a canonical four-state theory-revision waypoint.
Recovered automata reveal internal neural representations rather than observable behavioral shadows.

entries.label: Entry 02
entries.title: Exact symbolic planning held up, but rule invention could not say, “I do not know.”
entries.dek: The second set asks whether a fixed symbolic table can plan better than a neural model, detect when its world changes, and decide when to rewrite itself.

blocks.markdown:
**Does the symbolic machine really plan better?** At first, both the finite machine and neural beam search scored 100%. But the median plan was only three steps, and success counted if the target position appeared at any depth. The test was too easy. I changed it so the planner had to reach the exact final state at an exact sampled horizon. The 65-state symbolic machine stayed at **100%**. Neural beam search fell to **26.25%**, even though the neural model was still 99.90% accurate on random rollouts at horizon 128. The corrected test replaces the earlier easy claim.

**Can the model warn us before it leaves its known world?** A monitor tried to predict entry into a visible wind zone missing from the symbolic model. Using observation and action together gave AUROC .998 one step ahead and .922 twelve steps ahead. It ranked the risky plan above its paired safe plan 92.47% of the time. As a tie-breaker, it reduced actual exits from 47.5% to 22.25%. But it warned about only 74.5% of exits, and its false-positive rate on held-out safe cases was 5.78%, above the 5% validation target. When the change was unobservable, performance stayed at chance. This is a useful statistical warning, not a safety proof.

**Can the model re-ground itself after change?** After one shock, re-grounding reduced integrated error from 19.596 to 1.000 and recovered in every trial. A neural observer given the same information improved by exactly the same amount, so this does not show a uniquely symbolic advantage. A balanced escalation policy classified changes with 93.75% accuracy, made no false L1/L2 revisions, and revised 98.83% of permanent changes. With equal budgets, active repair covered more transitions and slightly improved global accuracy, 38.75% versus 36.11%, but it was worse on the policy's own data, 39.21% versus 51.19%. Neither method learned a good global table.

**When should a persistent change rewrite the theory?** An MDL gate solved the patch-growth problem, but only because I supplied the possible family of changes. During temporary shocks, naive patching grew to 118.36 states and planning fell to 86.69%. The gate kept 65 states and 100% planning. After a permanent force change, naive patching grew to 296.35 states and planning fell to 15.60%. The gate adopted one global rule after 33.91 steps and returned to 100%. Testing all 81 settings found 27 feasible choices, all with support 24. Once that much persistent support was available, extra confirmation probes only added delay and queries.

blocks.caption: The harder exact-horizon test revealed what random rollouts hid. The finite transition table planned successfully every time; neural beam search succeeded 26.25% of the time.

items.label: wrong adoption on both out-of-grammar controls

blocks.label: The decisive V6 boundary
blocks.markdown: When the true change belonged to the supplied grammar, both active and passive synthesis found it exactly in 97.5% of trials. Active learning did **not** beat passive learning, so registered prediction P2 failed. The more serious result came from two changes outside the grammar: parity and a random local table. The system adopted a wrong in-grammar approximation in every trial. Transition accuracy was only 54.7% and 56.2%; planning was 18.9% and 16.6%. It could search a supplied rule class, but it could not recognize that the whole class was wrong.

groups.title: Supported
items: A supplied-state finite machine can preserve exact long-horizon planning when a finite-width neural planner fails.
Prospective validity benefits from joint state/action context and can improve plan selection before a manifest contradiction.
Persistent-support gates can prevent transient overreaction and adopt a supplied compressed global change.

groups.title: Unsupported or failed
items: The prospective monitor provides formal safety.
Active V6 synthesis beats passive synthesis.
V6 detects or refuses dynamics outside its grammar.
The V6 run fully saved its declared artifacts; the archived execution stopped during CSV export.

entries.label: Entry 03
entries.title: Transfer scaled when the pieces were named in advance. Discovering the pieces from scratch failed.
entries.dek: The third set pushes the method into language, larger rule spaces, raw observations, exact testing, and programs too numerous to list one by one.

blocks.markdown:
**V10.1: an unfinished result.** On Tiny Shakespeare, the GRU had selection NLL 1.8934 while nanoGPT had 2.4527 at step 100 of 2,000. Then the run stopped during the next batch. It never produced a symbolic machine, hybrid gate, final validation, text generation, or registered verdict. The early NLL comparison is real, but it is not a completed crystallization experiment.

**V11: does quotient transfer save work?** Four reusable templates compressed 1,728 raw bits to 703.2 bits, a 2.46-fold reduction. Active and random search both needed a median of seven queries. At a fixed budget of eight, however, active search was exact in 100% of cases versus 78.1% for random. So active search improved the tail and fixed-budget success, not the median. For detecting new families by twelve queries, active scored 95.8%, while dual and random both scored 100%. A truly repeated new family was promoted after three worlds; none of twelve temporary worlds was promoted.

**V12: can an MDL state machine scale to text8?** In one pass, the retained state count grew from 24,902 at 1 million characters to 832,572 at 90 million. Test bits per character improved from 2.1736 to 1.6359, and top-1 accuracy reached 64.31%. Deep contexts of order at most 12 beat shallow contexts of order at most 4: 1.6359 versus 1.9762 bpc. Transition audits were exact. There was no neural baseline, so this is not a neural comparison. The source cell also contained two full revisions that wrote over the same artifact folder; the cleaned notebook separates them.

**V13 and V13.1: can neural guesses be corrected into an exact table?** The first BF16 program failed before training because it tried to add BF16 messages into float tensors. After that dtype error was fixed, V13.1 turned a local neural table with 47.57% accuracy into exact active crystallizations in 91.7% of trials, using a median of eight observations. It recovered all four recurring templates and reached 100% exact@8 on unseen cases. Increasing proposal top-k mattered: exact crystallization rose from 79.2% to 91.7%. An older V13 rerun and a nominally same-seed continuation both stopped early. Their small differences mean bit-for-bit GPU reproducibility was not established.

**V14: what happens when I stop naming the world for the learner?** I removed the supplied state labels and count, action-effect labels and count, family labels, and candidate grammar. Early mixture clustering looked good, with ARI .843. But behavioral ARI fell to .782, the exact number of states was recovered only 22.2% of the time, graph accuracy was 15.3%, and all twelve old graphs looked unique. No repeated grammar was learned. Active and random search both reached 33.3% exact, with median costs of 25 and 36. New families were never safely rejected or promoted. Registered predictions P1 through P8 all failed. The printed line `future exact=43/42` was only a sentinel for “not reached,” not 43 successes out of 42.

blocks.markdown:
**V16: how much of the difficulty comes from checking the answer?** With an exact synthetic equivalence oracle, simple suffix refinement recovered all 32 tested Moore machines, up to 24 states. Median membership queries rose from 89.5 for six states to 560 for 24. V16.1 replaced the perfect oracle with charged W-method tests and a supplied eight-state upper bound. Every ranking method eventually certified the right machine. Neural ranking used a median 829 interactions. That was 21.2% better than random, but **31.1% worse than simply trying shorter tests first**. The neural ranker had already cost 567,117 interactions to acquire; including that cost raised the amortized total to 18,551 interactions per test.

**V16.2: can verification scale when the program space cannot be listed?** From 20 to 80 program bits, Transformer token accuracy stayed near 98%, but exact whole-program proposals fell from 90.6% to 76.9%. The local MLP fell from 83.8% to 54.6%. Twenty random hashes followed by exact fallback gave 100% empirical correctness and accepted no wrong answer. For one fixed wrong proposal, the stated bound was $2^{-20}$. Still, fallback use and average query cost rose with program entropy. Absolute exactness required all $H$ identity bits. Training used 20,661,504 module observations, or 4,132 per test program after amortization. The module types, four-bit identities, reset operation, and parity-hash interface were all provided in advance.

groups.title: Supported
items: Quotient representations can compress and transfer deterministic finite laws across unseen coordinate relabelings.
Deep MDL-selected suffix states scale to text8 and improve held-out compression over shallow contexts.
Neural proposals can be error-corrected into exact finite tables when the ontology, grammar, query cells, and candidate budget are supplied.
Exact/PAC symbolic verification can be kept logically separate from a neural proposal score.

groups.title: Not supported
items: The Tiny Shakespeare hybrid completed or beat its components.
Active novelty search always beats random search.
The earlier transfer gains survive autonomous ontology and grammar acquisition.
Neural W-method ranking beats the shortest-test baseline or repays its prior-acquisition cost.
V16.2 demonstrates ontology-free, real-environment program discovery.

entries.label: Entry 04
entries.title: The method is useful under clear conditions. It is not yet an autonomous symbolic scientist.
entries.dek: The failures, controls, unfinished runs, and supplied interfaces are not footnotes. They define what the positive results mean.

blocks.markdown:
Here is the pattern I see. Finite-state learning, MDL compression, quotient transfer, and neural-to-symbolic extraction often work when the learner is given a clear contract. That contract may include a deterministic resettable world, named states and actions, a finite grammar or DSL, an upper bound on state count, exact membership questions, a parity-hash checker, or private ground truth for auditing. The results inside those contracts are real and useful.

Then come three boundary tests. In V14, removing the supplied ontology caused the whole pipeline to fail. In V6, an out-of-grammar world made the system confidently choose the wrong rule every time. In V16.1, neural test ranking lost to the simple “short tests first” rule and became very expensive when its training cost was counted. These failures do not cancel the successes. They show where the successes stop.

The word **exact** also needs care. Sometimes it means formal equivalence for a finite machine. Sometimes it means exact only under a stated state bound and test suite. Sometimes it means perfect accuracy on a finite or sampled audit. These are different claims. I also keep apart the evidence the learner could see from private ground truth used only for diagnosis. An unfinished run never enters the positive evidence count.

blocks.title: What I would test next, in order

items.name: Calibrated abstention outside the grammar
items.design: Repeat V6 with some new rules that fit the grammar and several families that do not. Give the learner an evidence threshold and let it answer “unknown.” Under the same budget, measure correct adoption, abstention, transition accuracy, and planning.
items.decisionValue: This asks whether the learner can avoid its 100% wrong-adoption failure before we make any larger open-world claim.

items.name: Factorized ontology recovery
items.design: Replace V14's clustering-first method with one that learns representations, chooses interventions, and refines predictive states together. Fix the train and test renderers in advance. Across several seeds, report the cost of finding the ontology as well as the later transfer cost.
items.decisionValue: This separates two explanations: perhaps V14 used the wrong bootstrap, or perhaps the available information was not enough.

items.name: Matched query-policy baselines
items.design: Compare neural, shortest-first, random, entropy-based, and hand-built structural rankings on exactly the same W-method tests. Count every training query, calibration step, reset, action, and second of wall time.
items.decisionValue: This tells us when learned ranking saves work overall, rather than merely beating random after its training cost has been hidden.

items.name: Multi-seed deterministic replication pack
items.design: Rerun selected CPU-exact and GPU-sensitive experiments in containers. Save dataset hashes, locked packages, generated worlds and splits, complete query transcripts, and paired deterministic/AMP runs.
items.decisionValue: This separates stable effects from paths caused by one seed, one GPU, or one numerical mode.

blocks.markdown:
Along this path, I learned that AI-assisted research has to be steered very carefully over the long run. When extending or interpreting results, a model is strongly biased by whatever is written in the prompt. Tell it to find a problem, and it finds one. Tell it to find a fix, and it finds one. Ask it to judge results against a hypothesis, and 100% of the time it says, “The results support it partially, but the negative result is more revealing; investigate the negative.” This can become a loop: negative finding, new branch, another negative finding, another branch.

The problem is how to make an LLM hold the research direction without adding that direction as a new bias in every prompt. The effect compounds. Tell it to scrutinize A, and it splits A into B, C, and D; decides D is wrong; then redirects the project toward D. I need better control mechanisms that maintain a constant direction and allow deviation only when I explicitly ask for it.

At the same time, I find myself taking more control over the research direction as my own knowledge grows. With recent advances such as GPT Astra, I am convinced that current state-of-the-art AI can genuinely help with research and make new connections. A tool like this makes it easier for me, as a human, to form higher-quality abductive hypotheses that may lead to real advances.
